# Nibbānadhātu Sutta (Iti 44 (It 2.17 PTS It 38))

**ID:** Iti 44 (It 2.17 PTS It 38)
**Section:** Itivuttaka (iti)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Nibbānadhātu Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Facets of Quenching
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/iti44

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nibbānadhātu Sutta* (Iti 44; PTS It 38–39) is a discourse in the *Itivuttaka* expounding the two facets or elements of quenching (*nibbānadhātu*): the *Nibbāna* element with residue remaining (*sa-upādisesā nibbānadhātu*) and the *Nibbāna* element without residue (*anupādisesā nibbānadhātu*) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2010]. In the prose exposition, the element with residue describes a living arahant who has eradicated lust, hatred, and delusion, yet whose five sense faculties (*pañcindriyāni*) remain intact, experiencing agreeable and disagreeable sensations; the element without residue describes the state where all feelings and experiences cool down right here (*idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissanti*) [Hwang 2005; Radich 2007; Pande 1974].

Scholars identify Iti 44 as the canonical *locus classicus* for this twofold formula, though it represents a unique and anomalous instance within the Pāli canon as the only text that directly formulates and discusses this overt contrast [Radich 2007]. Pande notes a doctrinal nuance between the prose and the verse portions of the sutta: while the prose seems to present the element without residue as attainable during life, the accompanying verse explicitly characterizes *anupādisesā* as pertaining to the beyond (*samparāyikā*), where all becomings cease entirely [Pande 1974]. This distinction has generated ongoing hermeneutical discussion: whereas classical Theravāda commentarial tradition equates the two respectively with the extinction of defilements in life (*kilesaparinibbāna*) and the remainderless cessation of the aggregates at death (*khandhaparinibbāna*), modern reformers such as Buddhadāsa have argued on the basis of Iti 44 that both terms refer to the living experience of arahants who "die to selfhood" before physical death [Kang 2012; Bodhi 2003].

Curated parallels recorded by SuttaCentral include Chinese versions in the *Ekottarika Āgama* (EĀ 16.2) and T 765.80 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates alignment with the *Ekottarika Āgama* (T 125, kṣudraka section) and detects cross-language matches in the Tibetan *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra* (D 301) and the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pāli canon, DharmaNexus records 211 text-reuse segments across 17 texts, sharing its longest matching sequences with the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3, AN 2, AN 4) and discourses in the *Majjhima Nikāya* (MN 112 and MN 76) [DharmaNexus].
